claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure.

A surrogate model combining DFT-derived misfit volumes, unstable stacking-fault energies, and hierarchical-microstructure descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture initiation behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate model will outperform conventional simulation methods.
Misfit volumes are relevant input parameters for models of alloy strengthening.
Surface and unstable stacking-fault energies are relevant input parameters for models of alloy ductility.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs local stress distributions and dislocation behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates the relationship between atomic-scale misfit energetics and macroscopic mechanical responses.
Combining DFT parameters with hierarchical-microstructure descriptors can approximate full-scale elastic and fracture simulations at substantially lower computational cost.
The proposed model can predict stress–strain responses and local fracture-initiation sites.
The model will predict Young’s modulus within ±5% error.
The model will predict yield strength within ±10% error.
The model will reliably identify fracture-initiation sites.
The model will reduce computation time by an order of magnitude relative to full DFT or continuum simulations.
Explicit DFT evaluation of fracture or yield strength in alloys is generally beyond currently available implementations.
First-principles simulations of the required parameters remain challenging for disordered multi-principal-element alloys.
Conventional continuum simulations have larger uncertainty in capturing fracture processes.
Major phase transformations, severe processing defects, environmental degradation, or inadequate representation of disordered local environments by DFT parameters may cause the model to fail.
Initial tests suggest that the proposed approach improves predictive speed and accuracy.
Accuracy and efficiency under extreme conditions or compositional variation remain uncertain and require further calibration.
